1:
The title and the authorship are settled by nobody. John Calvin observes that the prefixed preposition may be rendered either by or for, so that the ten psalms so inscribed may have been composed by the sons of Korah or merely committed to them; Calmet thought them composed by that family on grounds of style, others ascribe them to David and suppose he handed them to the chief musician to be sung by Korah’s posterity, and Calvin declines to decide. Adam Clarke allows that a descendant of Korah may have written it but says the occasion cannot now be discovered — the author aimed to be obscure, he adds, and has succeeded, for it is very difficult to make out his meaning. He also finds the psalm so much in the style of the book of Job that one might believe them to have the same author and this to have been part of that book, and quotes Dr. Dodd calling it a meditation on the vanity of riches and the haughtiness of those who possess them. Keil and Delitzsch agree on the kinship without the theory: the introduction recalls by its promissory tone the speeches of Elihu, while the dogmatic character and the antique, bold form rank the psalm with those of the time of David.

The summons is to everyone. Matthew Henry knows no more solemn introduction, and notes that the doctrine is not peculiar to those blessed with revelation, since the light of nature witnesses to it. Charles Ellicott says the two Hebrew terms answer to one another much as the Latin words for man and for a man, that the Greek and Latin take the first in its primary sense and render sons of the soil, and that Symmachus makes them stand for men in general and men as individuals. John Gill follows Ben Melech in taking the first for the common people, the base things of this world who are generally the ones called by grace, and the second for princes and nobles of illustrious extraction. C.H. Spurgeon distributes the profit: the low will be encouraged, the high warned, the rich sobered, the poor consoled. Augustine of Hippo hears the doubling as a demand for the ears of the heart, and wonders whether the nations are the wicked and those who dwell in the world the just.

What the psalmist proposes to open divides the last verse. Charles Ellicott gives the root idea of the word as similitude, notes that it is the term used of Balaam’s prophecies and of the speeches of Job, and adopts Ewald’s proverb-song, since the composition is meant for musical accompaniment; the dark saying comes either from a root meaning to tie, and so a knotty point, or to sharpen, and so an incisive one, while the Greek and Latin have problem. To open a riddle, he insists, is not to solve it but to propound it. John Wesley calls it properly an allegorical speech, often used for an important and withal dark sentence, and dark here because the thing in question has ever been thought hard to understand; to open it is not to smother it in his own breast but to publish it. Adam Clarke makes it a national habit: this was the general method of conveying instruction among the Asiatics, who used figure and metaphor to oblige men to think and reflect deeply, and the harp was there to soothe the animal spirits and prepare the mind for the prophetic influx. John Gill hears the manner in which Christ delivered out the doctrines of the Gospel. Charles Ellicott adds that the psalmist listens first, so as to catch the inspiration himself, as nature had an audible voice for Wordsworth.
5:
The evil that compasses the psalmist about is read four ways. Adam Clarke takes the word we render heels as a contracted plural meaning supplanters, so that the verse asks why he should fear though the iniquity of his supplanters compass him about; the Syriac and Arabic take a similar view, and Dr. Kennicott so translates it. John Wesley adopts the same word and finds it fits David’s enemies, who were not only malicious but deceitful and treacherous. Charles Ellicott objects: the received text seems to take heels for footsteps, as Symmachus does, and though that yields good sense it does not agree with the context; better that iniquity dogs him at the heels, wicked and prosperous men pursuing him with malice. He grants that the derived sense supplanter comes to the same thing, denies any direct reference to the bruising of the serpent, but allows that the heel as a vulnerable part, and wickedness lying like a snake in the path, may have occurred to the poet. C.H. Spurgeon takes exactly that: iniquity lies in wait like serpents that aim at the heels of travellers, and it was an old prophecy that the serpent should wound the heel of the woman’s seed. He knows the other renderings and prefers to keep to the received version where he can.

On the trust in wealth Matthew Henry is careful: it is not having riches that makes a man worldly, since a man may have abundance and be made better by it, and God often gives them to bad men, which shows they are not the best things in themselves. John Gill defines trusting as setting the eye and heart upon them and taking up rest in them, and lists what they cannot deliver from — present judgments, the sword, pestilence and famine, death, and the wrath to come. John Wesley marks the turn in the argument: having said the good have no cause of fear, the psalmist now shows the ungodly no cause for security. Charles Ellicott reads the brother in the wide sense of a fellow man, since death is the debt all owe and each must pay for himself, and God, in whose hand are the issues of life and death, is not to be bribed. Adam Clarke says it plainly, that wealth cannot save from death and God will not accept riches as a ransom.

The parenthesis about the redemption being precious produces the sharpest division in the psalm. John Gill, with Jarchi, renders the word heavy — heavier than their substance, too weighty a matter for the richest man to engage in — and finds the only price in the blood of Christ. Adam Clarke agrees that the soul is of too high a price to be redeemed with corruptible things, then proposes that the obscure clause be detached and joined to the following verse, yielding the sense that though he cease to be during the hidden time, yet he shall live on through eternity and not see corruption; this rendering, he claims, requires no alteration of the text, and is probably the dark saying the author designed to utter in a parable and leave to the ingenuity of posterity. Charles Ellicott shuts that door: the soul here is the animal life, as the context requires, and there is no anticipation of the Christian scheme of redemption from sin; the obscure clause means either that the ransom utterly fails or that the life utterly perishes and so cannot be ransomed, the Prayer Book taking the verb transitively, and the first is simplest. John Wesley keeps it flat: it is never to be accomplished by any mere man, for himself or for his brother.
10:
Charles Ellicott begins by redividing the clauses, which he says the received version gets wrong: on the contrary he must see it, the grave — wise men must die, likewise the fool and the stupid must perish — the wealth of the prudent availing no more for the prolonging of life than the wealth of fools. John Gill works the same point through the kinds of wisdom: worldly wise men who know how to get estates and provide for futurity, philosophers and physicians who know what preserves health and life, prudent magistrates and teachers who most deserve to live for their usefulness — all die. John Wesley notices the coldness of the phrase about leaving wealth: not to sons or kindred but to others, because the man is wholly uncertain whether it goes to friends, strangers or enemies.

The eleventh verse turns on two transposed letters. Adam Clarke says our version has patched out a sense by interpolation, and that the Greek translators appear to have used a copy in which the second and third letters of the word were reversed, giving graves for inward part: their sepulchres are their dwellings for ever. He cannot resist the arithmetic — six or seven feet long and two or three wide is enough to hold the greatest conqueror in the universe, a small house for the late possessor of numerous palaces and potent kingdoms. Charles Ellicott notes that eleven English words here represent three Hebrew, and holds that as the text stands the sense is intelligible and consistent, while the reading of the Greek, Chaldee and Syriac gives the other thought; the last clause, he adds, may mean that they are celebrated in their lands. John Gill reports the transposition too, and gives Aben Ezra’s rendering that their houses shall remain in the midst of their heirs. John Wesley is content with the plain sense: it is their secret hope, though they are ashamed to express it, and they name their lands fondly dreaming to immortalize their memories. Adam Clarke finds no evil in the naming itself, only in the infidel principle behind it, that they expected no state but the present.

The refrain divides them again. Charles Ellicott holds the Greek and Latin reading, without understanding in place of abideth not, unquestionably to be adopted: it brings the verse into exact correspondence with the last verse of the psalm, the Hebrew verb means to lodge temporarily and so could not express permanence, and the following verse is hardly intelligible without it. John Gill keeps the received sense but hears in it the first man, created in the image of God and crowned with glory, who lodged not a night in it — from which, he reports, some Jewish writers conclude that he fell the same day he was made. Adam Clarke reads it as warning rather than description: however rich, wise or honourable, they must die, and if they die without a sure hope of eternal life they die like beasts. John Wesley says their dreams of perpetuating name and estate shall be confuted by experience. C.H. Spurgeon presses the last clause hardest: their confidences are not casual aberrations but their regular course, and their posterity quote their worldly maxims and accept the mad career as prudence — grace is not hereditary, but sordid worldliness passes from generation to generation, and the race of fools never dies out.
14:
The fourteenth verse turns the flock over to a new shepherd. Keil and Delitzsch read the verb in a half-passive sense — like a herd of sheep they lay themselves down, or are made to lie down, into the underworld, shut up in it as sheep in their fold — and ask who rules them there with his rod: not the good Shepherd, whose pasture is the land of the living, but Death, personified as the king of terrors. Charles Ellicott agrees and calls the received rendering an error: it is not that death feeds on them but that death guides them, and he borrows Keble’s paraphrase, in which the flock is arrayed for the dark grave and death is their shepherd now. Adam Clarke keeps the feeding and sharpens it: death shall feed them — and with what? Damnation. He sets beside it Houbigant’s version, in which their morning shepherds rule over them and their flesh is to be consumed. C.H. Spurgeon takes both, death as a grim shepherd driving them to a pasturage of barrenness, and death as the monster of old stories that feeds on the men it entices to its cave. John Wesley divides the work between the two deaths, the first consuming their bodies and the second devouring their souls.

John Gill presses the comparison further than anyone: the likeness is not to sheep prepared for slaughter, since those are not thrown into a ditch, but, as Junius observes, to sheep that die of themselves, rotten sheep that are mere carrion and good for nothing else; and he adds the milder picture of a flock grazing in good pasture by day and penned at night in a dark and narrow fold. On the morning in which the upright have dominion John Wesley and C.H. Spurgeon agree that it is the resurrection — the saints who were the tail become the head at day-break, and this morning begins a day that does not end. Charles Ellicott calls the rest of the verse quite unintelligible as it stands, prefers the emendation of Burgess, by which the upright go down to the grave among the ungodly until the morning, and with a further change of points reads that their beauty is for corruption and the underworld its dwelling.

Whether the next verse answers the riddle divides the entry a last time. John Gill takes it of the resurrection outright: though the psalmist should die and lie for a while under the power of the grave, he will be redeemed from it in what will be for the saints the day of redemption, their bodies delivered from mortality and corruption; and he notes the alternative rendering, followed by the Targum, that the redemption is from the power of hell. Adam Clarke is briefer and no less certain: from the hand of the underworld, which by the plainest construction means a resurrection from the dead and an entrance into glory, with death having no dominion over him. Matthew Henry makes the same hope the support and joy of the children of God in a dying hour, and observes that the difference of outward condition, however great in life, makes none at death, while the difference of spiritual state, small now, is very great then. Charles Ellicott will go only so far: taken by itself the words might mean no more than being drawn back from the point of death, but taken with his rendering of the previous verse they are the dim foreshadowing of a better hope, that death did not altogether break the covenant bond — a hope towards which the Hebrew mind can be seen feeling its way through the later psalms and the book of Job.
16:
C.H. Spurgeon says the psalmist here turns preacher and gives admonitory lessons gathered from his own experience. Be not afraid, that is, let it give no concern to see the godless prosper; raise no questions about divine justice, since temporal prosperity is too small a matter to fret over — let the dogs have their bones. Those whose judgment is worthless esteem men the more for broader lands, and such estimates will find their level when truth and righteousness come to the fore. John Gill narrows the warning to a wicked rich man, one who neither fears God nor regards man and who seeks to be feared where he is not loved; from a good man no oppression is to be feared. John Wesley glosses the fear as discouragement. On the dying man carrying nothing away C.H. Spurgeon puts it as a leasehold that death ends: through the river of death a man passes naked, not a rag of his raiment nor a coin of his treasure going with him.

The self-congratulation of the eighteenth verse draws comment from all four. John Gill takes it of a man proclaiming himself happy because of his wealth and flattering himself with prosperity and length of days. John Wesley adds the chorus: as he flatters himself, so parasites flatter him for their own advantage. Charles Ellicott would render the second clause concessively, though men praise thee, and finds the whole abundantly illustrated by the parable of the rich fool. Adam Clarke turns it round on the reader: it is the custom of the world to praise those who pay most attention to their secular interest, while he who attends most to the concerns of his soul is deemed weak and foolish and is often persecuted for it.

Whether the light is ever seen again divides the close. Adam Clarke concedes the resurrection and withholds the glory: rise again they shall, but they shall never see the light of glory, for there is prepared for them the blackness of darkness for ever. Charles Ellicott renders it who will never again look on the light, that is, never live again — which he takes to imply, by contrast, a hope of resurrection for the upright. John Wesley denies both lights, this life to which they shall never return and the next to which they shall never be admitted, and has the man go to the grave and to his wicked parents, who led him into his evil courses by counsel and example. John Gill allows the phrase to mean the dwelling place of his fathers, grave or hell or both, or else that he may reach his fathers’ age and still must die at last. On the closing refrain Adam Clarke makes the man in honour without understanding a beast in God’s sight, and gives the maxim a civil edge: a man in a dignified official situation but destitute of learning and sound sense disgraces the place he occupies, like the beautifully carved head in the fable that was everything it should be and had no brains. John Wesley says the same shorter, that he has the outward shape of a man and is in truth a stupid creature. Adam Clarke ends by refusing an inference often drawn here, that the verb meaning to lodge for a night proves the first man fell the same day he was created and never spent a night in paradise: we may rest assured, he says, that this is no meaning of the text.
